title: Persona positioning matrix for engineering teams
content:
Purpose:
This is a working brief to align concise, testable messaging for three engineering personas we target: ML Engineers, Backend Engineers, and Platform Teams. Goal is to produce 1) short openers for marketing and SDRs, 2) a set of technical proof points and demos that resonate, and 3) objections + rebuttals tailored per persona.

Intended use: sales enablement snippets, landing page microcopy, product-led in-app onboarding CTAs, and A/B test variants for paid acquisition. Status: draft — rough language and open questions highlighted.

High-level differentiation we want each persona to hear:
- ML engineers: "Predictable, low-latency inference with model-aware optimizations so your experiments scale from prototype to prod without revisiting infra decisions."
- Backend engineers: "Drop-in API with predictable p99 latency and automatic fallbacks — integrate like any other service and avoid surprises under load."
- Platform teams: "Unified runtime with policy-based routing, capacity guarantees, and observability you can integrate into your infra standards."

Quick elevator lines (30–50 char variants for UI or subject lines):
- ML: "From notebook to 1000qps — inference that scales."
- Backend: "An API engineered for production SLOs."
- Platform: "Control plane for predictable LLM serving."

Messaging scaffold (what to emphasize per persona)
1) ML engineers — priorities and proof points
   - Priorities: reproducible outputs, easy model swapping, cost-aware perf, quick experiments -> production path.
   - Proof points to surface: model catalog + verified perf runs, per-token cost breakdown, examples of quantized model parity for common tasks, quick rollout snippet showing pinning model versions.
   - Demo idea: "Experiment to Production" notebook that calls Redwood SDK, swaps a model variant and flips a canary via the same config file.
   - Tech-speak: show perf numbers on GPT-like open models (e.g., 25ms median for "small-chat" variant at 256 token context with batching enabled) and quantization options.
   - Objections + rebuttals:
     * "I can run open models myself." => "You can — but our smart routing, KV cache, and continuous batching typically reduce token cost by 30–60% at scale; plus you avoid engineering time for fallbacks and SLA ops."
     * "I need reproducible logits / deterministic outputs." => "Support for pinned model versions, deterministic decoding flags, and replayable request tracing for debug."

2) Backend engineers — priorities and proof points
   - Priorities: latency SLOs, simple integration, predictable billing, retry/fallback behavior.
   - Proof points to surface: p50/p95/p99 latencies across common payloads, SDK examples in languages (Go/Java/Python) with <10 lines to call, automatic retry and fallback policy example using routing by cost vs latency.
   - Demo idea: microservice example: endpoint that proxies requests to Redwood, shows graceful fallback to smaller model in heavy load while maintaining 50ms p95.
   - Tech-speak: emphasize stable HTTP/REST + streaming, crates/SDKs compatibility, and token-level cost attribution.
   - Objections + rebuttals:
     * "We can’t accept variable latencies from multi-tenant APIs." => "Dedicated capacity and reserved pools are available; we publish benchmarks and offer per-route SLA options so you can set expected tail latencies."
     * "Cost is unpredictable." => "Showing cost-control levers: batching windows, prefix caching, model quantization profiles, and cost alerts integrated into Console."

3) Platform teams — priorities and proof points
   - Priorities: governance, capacity planning, observability, security/compliance.
   - Proof points to surface: VPC/private deployment options, KMS/HSM integration notes, audit log examples, capacity reservation policies and autoscaling controls with predictable throughputs.
   - Demo idea: onboarding checklist that hooks Redwood Console into an SRE team’s observability stack (example: open tracing + Prometheus exporter + example dashboard JSON).
   - Tech-speak: policy-based routing examples (by region, latency, or cost tier), rollout primitives (canary/A-B/auto-fallback), and per-token audit trails.
   - Objections + rebuttals:
     * "We must keep everything inside our VPC/on-prem." => "Private deploy with customer-managed control plane, plus air-gapped options and documented deployment checklist for SOC/ISO audits."
     * "We need to own scaling behavior and capacity guarantees." => "Reserved Dedicated pools, explicit autoscaling policies, and regional failover policies combined with SLO-backed contracts."

Cross-persona shared proof assets (short list to create / update)
- Benchmark matrix CSV: model variant, tokens/context, median/p95/p99, batch sizes tested. (linked to GitHub benchmark doc)
- One-page cheat sheet: "How to think about latency vs cost" targeted for engineers (500 words + annotated graphic).
- Sample SDK snippets in Go/Java/Python + small end-to-end deploy example.
- Console screenshots focused per persona: ML (model catalog + version pinning), Backend (per-route latency/cost breakdown), Platform (routing & audit logs).

Competitive notes (quick callouts for sales and product marketing)
- Managed cloud vendors (large cloud GP U offerings): Strength = infra scale, weakness = lack of LLM-aware runtime optimizations and model lifecycle features. Message: "We’re engineered for LLM serving — not general VM/container mgmt."
- LLM API providers (simplicity-first): Strength = small onboarding friction. Weakness = unpredictable tail latency at scale and limited deployment modes. Message: "Same simple API but with predictable SLOs and options for Dedicated/Private."
- Self-hosted runtimes/open-source stacks: Strength = control. Weakness = engineering cost to get production-grade batching, KV caches, and fallbacks. Message: "Avoid re-building maintenance-heavy pieces; we give a plug-in path with ops controls."

Examples of short talk tracks for SDRs and AE use (30–90s)
- ML engineer SDR script (30s): "Hey — quick question: when you move models from notebook to prod, do you spend engineering cycles rewriting inference logic? Redwood gives you a model-aware runtime with caching and batching so your experiments keep working as traffic grows — here’s a 5-min notebook you can run against your data."
- Backend engineer AE script (60s): "We help teams treat LLMs like regular services — predictable p99s, built-in retry/fallback, and language SDKs. Many customers replace ad-hoc proxy layers and regain 20–40% in token-cost efficiency after enabling prefix caching and smart batching."
- Platform lead AE script (90s): "If you’re evaluating LLMs for product teams, the hard part isn’t a single model — it’s operating the set of models reliably. Redwood provides reserved pools, routing policies, and audit trails so platform owners can enforce governance while teams iterate on models. Can I walk you through our reserved capacity and KMS integration in 20 minutes?"

A/B test ideas and measurable signals
- Landing page headline variants: emphasize cost-efficiency vs. latency vs. governance. Metric: click-to-signup and time-to-first-API-call.
- Trial flow CTA variants: "run a 3-minute notebook" vs "set up dedicated trial capacity". Metric: completion rate and conversion to paid.
- Sales pitch test: include 1-line latency guarantee vs generic "production-ready" language. Metric: boolean conversion to demo request.

Unresolved questions / decision points
- How many concrete latency datapoints can we publicly publish per model family without violating benchelling policy? (Action: check legal/bench team — JIRA-MLMSG-134)
- Which SDK snippets should be the canonical 1-line call for each language? (Action: devex to pick canonical minimal examples)
- Do we create separate landing flows for ML vs Backend vs Platform at top-level marketing? (Action: growth to propose funnel layout by 2025-03-10)

Next steps (owners assigned)
- Create one-page cheat sheet for engineers (owner: Priya Desai, due: 2025-03-07).
- Produce three 2-minute demo videos (owner: Ethan Rivera, due: 2025-03-14).
- Legal check on benchmark publication policy (owner: Maya Thompson, due: 2025-03-04).
- Wire up A/B experiments with Growth for two headline variants (owner: Luca Romano, due: 2025-03-10).

Notes to self / rough language to iterate on
- Keep statements quantifiable where possible (p99 X ms, cost Y per 1M tokens).
- Prioritize concrete examples over superlatives for engineering audiences.
- Put governance & security language earlier for platform-focused collateral.

Slack threads / references worth reading (internal):
- #bench-results: last summary 2025-02-17 (perf runs for quantized variants)
- #sre-oncall: notes on fallback behaviors for a recent incident 2025-01-29
- Confluence: gtm/persona-library (linked above)

Draft checklist for finalization before publishing:
- Bench CSV attached + source scripts
- Legal signoff on published numbers
- DevEx approved SDK snippets and code formatting
- Growth created experiment pages and UTM tracking
- Sales enablement one-pager with objection handlers and links to demos

End of draft.
